title: Prey for Rock and Roll
full_review:
Director Alex Steyermark's raw drama "Prey for Rock and Roll" (MAC) asks how old is too old before you should hang up your electric guitar, but the answer is less than satisfying.

Gina Gershon stars as Jacki, the lead singer-guitarist of an all-girl punk rock band in Los Angeles which includes bassist Tracy (Drea De Matteo), lead guitarist Faith (Lori Petty) and drummer Sally (Shelly Cole). The band is still struggling, playing dive gigs and working for pennies. So for Jacki, clad in leather pants and dark eyeliner, celebrating her 40th birthday means asking herself, "At what point do I become a joke?"

The story is based on Cheri Lovedog's autobiographical rock musical about her days in the female quartet named Clamdandy. Gershon's strong performance carries the film for a while, but she cannot go the distance with the poorly written script.

A major problem with the script, written by Lovedog and Robin Whitehouse, is that it has no real story to tell. Instead, the film toils along with melodramatic plot machinations and cliched views about aging in the young world of music. The compelling question of whether or not to hold on to the rock 'n' roll dream of fame and fortune, despite the onset of middle age, hangs in the air. The screen meanwhile is filled with obvious ploys, such as a rape-revenge scenario and the death of a character, to keep viewers interested in what is otherwise a droning tale.

However, even putting this cinematic flaw aside, "Prey for Rock and Roll" has a larger obstacle to overcome as far as Catholic audiences are concerned. The film's casual acceptance of both the lesbian and bisexual lifestyles cannot be ignored.

Jacki hasn't decided which "team" she will play for. A fairly graphic sexual scene shows Jacki and her girlfriend in compromising positions. But later on she falls for Animal (Marc Blucas), the brother of one of her band mates -- and an ex-con recently released from prison. And troubled trust-fund baby Tracy has a clear substance abuse problem that leads her to perform certain sexual acts in exchange for drugs.

"Prey for Rock and Roll" rarely allows the audience to sympathize with the characters because it never goes beyond the surface.

Due to some sexual encounters including a same-sex scene, brief violence, intermittent drug abuse and recurring rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
